stem: Ada wants to read the full reference for the `cp` command on the machine itself. Which command opens it?

options.rationale: `help` documents only Bash builtins, and `cp` is an external program.
`which` prints the path of the program, not its documentation.
`man` opens the manual page of the named command in a pager.
`apropos` searches page descriptions and lists matches; it opens nothing.

explanation: `man NAME` shows the manual page in a pager. The page has the command’s synopsis and every option, and it works offline.

stem: Mira opened `man ls` and wants to leave the page. Which key quits the pager?

options.rationale: The pager quits when you press q.
This key does nothing special in the man pager.
Enter scrolls down by one line.
Tab is not bound to anything useful in the pager.

explanation: `man` shows pages through a pager (usually `less`). Space and `f` go forward, `b` goes back, `/` searches and `q` quits.

stem: While reading a man page, Jonas wants to find the word “human” in it. Which input starts a forward search?

options.rationale: `q` quits the pager, so nothing is searched.
`h` opens the pager’s own help screen.
`f` moves one page forward and takes no search text.
A slash starts a forward search in the pager, and `n` jumps to the next hit.

explanation: Inside the pager, `/text` searches forward, `n` goes to the next match and `N` to the previous one.

stem: Which manual section holds file formats and configuration files such as `/etc/passwd`?

options.rationale: Section 1 covers user commands.
Section 5 describes file formats and conventions.
Section 8 covers system administration commands.
Section 3 covers library functions for programmers.

explanation: The common sections are 1 (user commands), 5 (file formats and configuration files) and 8 (administration commands). `man 5 passwd` shows the file format.

stem: Mira runs `man passwd` and reads about changing a password, but she wants the description of the `/etc/passwd` file. What should she run?

options.rationale: The section must come before the page name.
Putting the section number before the name selects section 5, the file format.
`-5` is not an option to select a section.
There is no such option; the section number is how you choose.

explanation: The same name can exist in several sections. `man` shows the first match, here section 1, the command. `man 5 passwd` asks for the file format.

stem: What does `man -k copy` do?

options.text: It searches inside the full text of every man page for “copy”
options.rationale: Only names and short descriptions are searched, not the page bodies.

options.text: It opens the man page named `copy` in section k
options.rationale: `-k` is not a section; it selects the keyword search.

options.text: It lists the files on disk whose names contain “copy”
options.rationale: File names are searched with `find`; `man -k` knows only the manual database.

options.text: It searches the names and short descriptions of all man pages for the word “copy”
options.rationale: The `-k` option is a keyword search over the one-line descriptions.

explanation: `man -k WORD` (the same as `apropos WORD`) is the way to find a command whose name you can’t remember. It matches names and one-line descriptions.

stem: Which command is equivalent to `man -k`?

options.rationale: `apropos WORD` does a keyword search in the descriptions.
`whatis` is the same as `man -f`: it looks up an exact name.
`whereis` locates the binary, source and manual files of a command.
`mandb` builds the database that these searches use; it doesn’t search.

explanation: `apropos` and `man -k` are the same search; `whatis` and `man -f` are the same lookup of an exact name.

stem: Jonas wants a one-line description of exactly the command `tar`, not a list of every page that mentions it. Which command does this?

options.rationale: `man -w` prints the file path of the page, not its description.
This matches every description that contains “tar”, a longer list.
`whatis` prints the short description of pages with exactly that name.
That prints the version of the program, not a description.

explanation: `whatis NAME` (or `man -f NAME`) shows the one-line description from the page’s NAME section for exact name matches.

stem: In the SYNOPSIS `cp [OPTION]... SOURCE DEST`, what do the square brackets and the three dots mean?

options.text: `OPTION` is required, and it can be used once only
options.rationale: Required parts are shown without brackets.

options.text: `OPTION` is a file name, and it must be typed in capitals
options.rationale: Upper case words are placeholders for real values and are not typed as shown.

options.text: `OPTION` is optional, and it can be repeated
options.rationale: Brackets mark something optional; dots mean more of the same.

options.text: `OPTION` is a comment, and the shell ignores it
options.rationale: The shell doesn’t read the manual notation; it’s just a convention.

explanation: In synopsis notation, `[ ]` means optional, `...` means “one or more of these” and upper-case words are placeholders you replace with real values.

stem: Where do the manual pages of a Debian system live?

options.text: In directories under `/usr/share/man/`, one per section
options.rationale: Compressed pages are stored in `man1`, `man5` and the other section directories.
This holds extra package documentation such as README files, not the man pages.

options.text: In `/etc/man/`, next to the configuration files
options.rationale: No: `/etc` is for configuration files.
`/var` holds variable data such as logs, not manual pages.

explanation: `man -w NAME` prints the file a page is read from, for instance `/usr/share/man/man1/mkdir.1.gz`. The pages are gzip compressed, one directory per section.

stem: Besides man pages, packages install extra documentation such as README files, changelogs and example configuration files. Where?

options.rationale: This directory holds the man pages themselves.
No such standard directory exists; `/etc` is for configuration.
`/var/lib` holds program state, not documentation.
Each package gets its own subdirectory here.

explanation: `/usr/share/doc/NAME/` usually holds README files, `copyright`, `changelog.gz` and sometimes an `examples` folder. Files ending in `.gz` can be read with `zcat`.

stem: Before changing a service’s settings, Mira wants a sample configuration file for the package `foo`. Where should she look first?

options.rationale: `/usr/bin` holds executables, not sample files.
Package documentation and sample files are installed under the package’s doc directory.
Packages don’t get a home directory under `/home`.
Logs show what happened; they are not templates for configuration.

explanation: Many packages ship sample configuration files in `/usr/share/doc/PACKAGE/` (often in `examples`). They make a good starting point for your own file.

stem: Which command prints a short usage summary of `ls` without opening the manual?

options.rationale: `ls` has no `--manual` option, so this is an error.
`--help` makes most GNU tools print a usage summary and exit.
This is not a valid option for `ls`.
`ls` doesn’t implement `--usage`.

explanation: Most command line tools accept `--help`. The text starts with a `Usage:` line, similar to the SYNOPSIS of the man page, and then lists the options.

stem: Ada types `df -h` and sees sizes like `1.2G`. What does `-h` mean here?

options.text: Show a help text for the command
options.rationale: Help is requested with `--help`; `-h` isn’t help in `df`.

options.text: Hide the header line of the table
options.rationale: There is no option to hide the header with `-h`.
`-h` doesn’t filter by hidden status.
In `ls` and `df`, `-h` stands for “human-readable”.

explanation: `-h` is not always “help”. In `ls -lh` and `df -h` it means human-readable sizes. `--help` is the dependable way to ask for usage.

stem: Why does `man cd` print “No manual entry for cd”, even though `cd` works?

options.text: `cd` is a Bash builtin and has no page of its own; `help cd` explains it
options.rationale: Builtins are documented by the shell’s `help` command and in the Bash manual.

options.text: `cd` is a hidden command that only root may read about
options.rationale: Nothing is hidden: any user can read manual pages.

options.text: `cd` is stored in section 9, which is not installed
options.rationale: The page doesn’t exist in any section, because it is not a separate program.

options.text: `man` can only show pages of programs that were written in C
options.rationale: The language a program is written in is irrelevant to man pages.

explanation: Bash builtins such as `cd` are part of the shell. Use `help cd` for a short description, or read the shell’s own man page, `man bash`.

stem: What does `--version` usually do when it is given to a command like `cp`?

options.text: It lists the file versions that were backed up
options.rationale: `--version` is unrelated to backups or file versions.

options.text: It opens the manual page for the newest version
options.rationale: It prints a short text and doesn’t open the manual.

options.text: It prints the program’s version information and exits
options.rationale: GNU tools print their name and version and do nothing else.

options.text: It updates the program to the latest version
options.rationale: Programs don’t update themselves through this option.

explanation: `--version` prints the program name and version, for example `cp (GNU coreutils) 9.1`, and exits without doing any work.

stem: Which command opens the info pages for the GNU `coreutils` package?

options.rationale: This would look for a man page named `info` in section `coreutils`.
`help` shows Bash builtins only.
`info NAME` opens the info document for that name.
`apropos` searches page descriptions, and opens no document.

explanation: `info NAME` opens the info document. GNU projects often keep more complete documentation there than in a man page.

stem: In an `info` document, which key goes to the next node?

options.rationale: `n` moves to the next node, `p` to the previous one.
`q` quits the info reader.
`u` goes up to the parent node.
`p` goes to the previous node.

explanation: Info text is split into nodes: `n` next, `p` previous, `u` up, Enter follows a menu link, `/` searches and `q` quits.

stem: How do info pages differ from man pages?

options.text: An info document is a single flat page that is shown in a pager
options.rationale: That describes man pages.

options.text: An info document can be read only by the root user
options.rationale: Any user can read them.

options.text: An info document is stored as a graphic file and shown in a browser
options.rationale: Info pages are text and are read in the terminal.

options.text: An info document is split into linked nodes that you can navigate like a small website
options.rationale: The reader follows links between nodes with Enter and moves with `n`, `p` and `u`.

explanation: Man pages are single pages with a fixed layout. Info documents are organised in nodes with menus and cross references and are read with the `info` command.

stem: Ada created a file a few minutes ago, but `locate` does not find it. Why?

options.text: `locate` only searches files that are larger than one megabyte
options.rationale: It has no size limit like that.

options.text: `locate` searches a prebuilt database that is only updated periodically
options.rationale: New files appear only after the database has been refreshed.

options.text: `locate` searches inside file contents, not names
options.rationale: It searches file names, and `grep` searches contents.

options.text: `locate` ignores any file that Ada owns
options.rationale: Ownership doesn’t matter for the database search.

explanation: `locate` is fast because it looks up a database of file names. The database is rebuilt by a regular job, or by hand with `updatedb`, so it can miss new files and still list deleted ones.

stem: Which command, run by root, rebuilds the database that `locate` uses?

options.rationale: `mandb` rebuilds the manual page index, not the file-name database.
`updatedb` scans the file system and rewrites the file-name database.
`ldconfig` updates the shared library cache.
`apt update` refreshes the package lists from the repositories.

explanation: `updatedb` refreshes the database, which most systems also do daily. The command `mandb` refreshes the man page database that `man -k` uses.

stem: Mira needs a file name search that always reflects the current state of the disk, including files created a minute ago. Which command should she use?

options.rationale: `locate` uses a database that can be hours old.
`updatedb` rebuilds the database; it doesn’t search.
`whatis` looks up manual page descriptions, not files.
`find` walks the real file system, so its results are always current.

explanation: `find` is slower than `locate` but has no database to go stale. `locate` is quick but only as current as its last `updatedb`.

stem: Which commands search the short descriptions of man pages for a keyword? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: A keyword search over the descriptions.
The same keyword search under another name.
This only looks up pages with exactly that name.
This prints the path of the page named `copy`.
This opens the page named `copy` in section 1, if it exists.

explanation: `man -k` and `apropos` are the same keyword search. `whatis` and `man -f` look up a page by its exact name, and `man -w` prints its location.

stem: Which statements about manual sections are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Section 1 holds user commands such as `ls`
options.rationale: Section 1 is for commands you run.

options.text: Section 5 holds file formats and configuration files
options.rationale: For example `man 5 passwd`.
Games are section 6; section 8 is system administration.
Section 3 covers library functions for programmers.

options.text: The section number goes after the page name
options.rationale: It goes before: `man 5 passwd`.

explanation: Sections: 1 user commands, 2 system calls, 3 library functions, 4 special files, 5 file formats, 6 games, 7 miscellaneous, 8 administration. The number is given before the name.

stem: Which of these are typically found in `/usr/share/doc/PACKAGE/`? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Package documentation is installed here.
Often in an `examples` folder.
Programs are installed under `/usr/bin` and similar directories.
These are in `/usr/share/man/`.
Logs are written below `/var/log`.

explanation: `/usr/share/doc/` holds the extras: README, `copyright`, `changelog.gz` and examples. Programs, man pages and logs have their own places.

stem: Which of these show help for the command `cp`? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Prints a usage summary.
Opens the full manual page.
`help` only knows Bash builtins.
This option does not exist.
`-m` isn’t a help option.

explanation: `cp --help` is quick; `man cp` is complete. `help` is for builtins like `cd`.

stem: Which statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: `info` reads info documents made of linked nodes
options.rationale: The reader moves between nodes.

options.text: `locate` searches a database of file names
options.rationale: It is fast, but the database may be outdated.

options.text: `locate` searches the real disk every time it runs
options.rationale: It reads a database instead.
Man pages are read with `man`.

options.text: `updatedb` shows the manual page of a command
options.rationale: `updatedb` rebuilds the file-name database used by `locate`.

explanation: `info` reads GNU’s info documents. `locate` is fast because it reads a prebuilt database that `updatedb` refreshes.

stem: Type the command that opens the manual page of `mkdir`.
explanation: `man mkdir` opens the page in a pager. Quit it with `q`.

stem: Finish the command so that it lists every man page whose short description contains the word `copy`.
explanation: `man -k copy` is the keyword search. `apropos copy` does the same.

stem: Type the command that shows the manual page about the file format of `/etc/passwd`, not the `passwd` command.
explanation: The section number comes first. Section 5 holds file formats, section 1 the commands.

stem: Type the long option that makes most GNU commands print a usage summary.
explanation: `--help` prints usage information and exits. Many tools also accept `-h`, but it isn’t reliable: `ls -h` means human-readable sizes.

stem: Bash builtins have no man page. Type the builtin command that describes the builtin `cd`.
explanation: `help cd` prints a description of the builtin. External programs use `--help` or `man`.

stem: Type the absolute path of the directory with one subfolder of extra documentation per installed package.
explanation: `/usr/share/doc/` holds README files, licences, change logs and examples.

stem: Type a command that prints the one-line description of `grep`.
explanation: `whatis grep` and `man -f grep` look up the exact name and print the one-line description.

stem: Type the command that opens the info document of `ls`.
explanation: `info ls` jumps to the `ls` node of the coreutils info document. Leave with `q`.

stem: Jonas looks up exactly one name. What does this command print?

options.rationale: `whatis` prints name, section and the one-line description of `mkdir`.
That is the description of `rmdir`.
The command is in section 1, not 5.
That is the file location, printed by `man -w`.

explanation: The line shows the page name, its section in brackets and the short description from the NAME section.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: `man -w` prints the path of the page file instead of showing it. Pages are gzip-compressed and live in `/usr/share/man/man1/` for section 1.

stem: What does this command print?

options.rationale: The real synopsis marks both parts as repeatable with `...`.
This is the header of the man page, not the `--help` text.
The first line of the usage text is the synopsis, with `[OPTION]...` and `[FILE]...` marking repeatable parts.
`--help` is a valid long option for `ls`.

explanation: The `Usage:` line is the same synopsis the man page shows. Piping the output through `head` keeps only the first line.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: `help NAME` prints the usage of a Bash builtin. The first line shows the builtin’s name and its options, `-L` and `-P`.

stem: Mira asks for the manual page of a Bash builtin. What does this command print?

options.rationale: No such page exists, so there is no header to show.
That is what `help cd` prints.
Builtins have no man page of their own, so `man` reports that no entry exists.
No man page, and so no description, exists for `cd`.

explanation: Use `help cd` for Bash builtins. `man` knows only external programs, files and concepts that have a page.

stem: Type what this command prints.
explanation: The pattern `^rmdir$` matches only the page whose name is exactly `rmdir`, so one line is printed with its section and description.

stem: Jonas is deep inside a long man page and has just passed the part he needed. Which key sequence searches backward from his position?

options.rationale: Correct: `?` searches backward, and `n` or `N` then continue the search.
`/` searches forward, towards the end of the page.
`b` scrolls back one screen; it does not search for text.
`h` opens the pager's help screen.

explanation: The pager (usually `less`) uses `/` to search forward and `?` to search backward. `n` repeats the search in the same direction and `N` in the opposite one.

stem: Mira searched a man page with `/option` and wants to jump to the next match. Which key does that?

options.rationale: `q` quits the pager.
`g` goes to the top of the page.
Space scrolls down one screen; it does not jump to a match.
Correct: `n` repeats the last search in the same direction.

explanation: After a search, `n` finds the next match in the same direction and `N` the previous one.

stem: Which program does `man` normally use to show a page one screen at a time?

options.rationale: Correct: that is why `q`, `/` and Space work in a man page.

options.text: `cat`, which prints the file in one go
options.rationale: `cat` would not let you scroll or search.
`info` is a separate reader for a different format.
Man pages are shown read-only; an editor is not the default.

explanation: `man` pipes the formatted page through a pager, most often `less`. That is why the same keys work as in `less`.

stem: Ada is looking for the man section that describes the kernel's internal routines. It is rarely installed and not part of the standard layout. Which section number is it?

options.rationale: Section 2 describes system calls, the kernel functions programs can call.
Section 4 describes special files, mostly in `/dev`.
Correct: section 9 is the non-standard section for kernel routines.
Section 7 holds conventions and overviews, not kernel internals.

explanation: Sections 1 to 8 are the standard ones. Section 9, kernel routines, is marked non-standard in the `man` manual page and is often missing.

stem: Where does a Debian system keep the READMEs, change logs and licence files that come with each installed package?

options.text: In one directory per package under `/usr/share/doc/`
options.rationale: Correct: for example `/usr/share/doc/bash`.

options.text: In `/usr/share/man/`, next to the man pages
options.rationale: That directory holds the man pages themselves.

options.text: In the `/etc` directory, with the configuration
options.rationale: `/etc` holds configuration files, not documentation.

options.text: In the `/var/doc` directory, managed by cron
options.rationale: There is no such standard directory.

explanation: Packages install their extra documentation in `/usr/share/doc/<package>`, and the package manager manages those files.

stem: Mira wants a quick reminder of the options of `cp`, not the long manual. What is the best fit?

options.rationale: Correct: it prints a short usage summary and the list of options.
This searches the descriptions of all man pages for the word.
`cp` has no directory of that name; it is part of a larger package.
This prints only the version of the program.

explanation: `--help` gives the usage line and the options at a glance. The man page is the full reference.
